children: By James Pomfret

"For the first time in history, we, the people of Hong Kong, will be master of our own destiny." On July 1, 1997, Tung Chee-hwa delivered his first speech as chief executive of the territory, following its handover from the United Kingdom to China.

"The Special Administrative Region Government is fully committed to preserving the Hong Kong way of life, maintaining Hong Kong's free and open economic system, upholding the rule of law, and building a more democratic society," he said.

Six years later, Tung sought to push through Article 23. The proposed security law, covering offences like treason and sedition while expanding police powers, was widely seen as Chinese encroachment on Hong Kongers' freedoms.
It triggered a half-million-strong protest, with many demonstrators wearing black as a sign of mourning.

Tung backed down. But the events of 2003 set the stage for increased tensions between opposition democrats and Beijing over the city's future. These eventually boiled over with major, months-long pro-democracy movements in 2014 and 2019.
Tung's ill-fated Article 23 bill was eventually approved in  March 2024 by a predominantly pro-Beijing legislature.

A former shipping tycoon, Tung Chee-hwa led Hong Kong as it emerged from more than 150 years of British colonial rule and adopted the "one country, two systems" principle, whereby the territory rejoined China but was afforded a high degree of autonomy from the mainland authorities.
His time in office also showed the limits of that principle.
He died on Tuesday aged 89, South China Morning Post reported, citing a statement from his office. No cause of death was given.
PLUNGING POPULARITY
The scion of Orient Overseas Container Line, an international shipping empire founded by his father, Tung enjoyed close ties to China's leaders during the 1990s, including then-President Jiang Zemin.
In December 1996, Tung was chosen by a 400-person committee stacked with Beijing loyalists to become the city's first leader under Chinese rule.
"We will maintain Hong Kong as a vibrant and international city," Tung said in his inaugural speech.
But Tung, who lacked any previous political experience, soon struggled with the demands of public office.
Hong Kongers' aspirations for greater democracy were at odds with gradual moves by Beijing to tighten control of the free-wheeling international financial hub.
After the blunt 2003 push to enact Article 23 by Tung and his security chief, Regina Ip, the chief executive's popularity ratings plunged.
The national security bill was shelved. He resigned two years later, halfway through his second term, citing ill health.
That protest became a turning point for Hong Kong's relations with China, with Beijing increasingly unnerved by what it saw as anti-China forces seeking to undermine national sovereignty.
Beijing began to restrict the scope of democratic reforms to ensure its continued control.
INFLUENTIAL BEHIND THE SCENES

Tung Chee-hwa was born in Shanghai in July 1937, the son of shipping magnate Tung Chao-yung and Koo Lee-ching, herself reportedly the daughter of a prominent shipowner. The family moved to Hong Kong when he was a child.

As an adult, he spent significant time in the West, attending the University of Liverpool in England, during which time he became a lifelong supporter of Liverpool Football Club. In the U.S., he worked for General Electric and later the family business.

After stepping down as Hong Kong's leader, Tung was given a second lease of political life when he was appointed as a vice chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body.
He was considered influential behind the scenes.
Tung and his father had been longtime friends of former U.S. president George Bush, with the younger Tung also building a rapport with President George W. Bush.

When Xi Jinping visited the U.S. in 2012, just before becoming China's leader, he was accompanied by Tung. In 2015, when President Xi visited Washington, Tung also joined the delegation in an unofficial capacity.
But Tung's elder-statesman credentials as a bridge between the two countries waned as bilateral relations began to worsen.

His China-U.S. Exchange Foundation - a Hong Kong-based non-profit that made grants to U.S. universities and courted politically influential Washingtonians - came under fire for having ties to the Chinese government. A 2018 U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission report said it had  "involvement in influence operations".
'HAPPINESS AND WELLBEING FOR THE PEOPLE'

When large-scale pro-democracy protests flared up in Hong Kong in 2019, Tung became increasingly outspoken, describing protesters as "anti-China disruptors" who had "gravely" endangered national security.
The demonstrators carried umbrellas to shield themselves from police tear gas and rubber bullets.
Tung also defended a sweeping national security law imposed by China on Hong Kong in 2020 that some countries, including the U.S., described as a draconian tool of repression.
In recent years, Tung largely disappeared from the public eye.

In one of his last interviews, with the Chinese Communist Party-aligned People's Daily newspaper, he backed a 2021 overhaul of the city's electoral system that effectively shut out opposition democrats from future elections.
"The ultimate test for any method of election is whether it brings happiness and wellbeing for the people," Tung said.
"But only restoring social stability is not enough. We now need to strive for prosperity."
